downloads.detail: The deck from Andrea's personal statement workshop, updated July 2026. Thirty-six slides: do's and don'ts, topics to avoid, how to build an introduction, body and conclusion, writing strategies from verb tense to pacing, the 2026 to 2027 Common App prompts, and the brainstorming questions she asks students first.

reads.title: Six things to do before you write a word

items.text: Start early. Revising is where essays get good, and revising takes time.
Brainstorm and outline first. Write down the strengths, interests and quirks you want admissions officers to know about.
Make it your own. Write about what you care about, not what you think they want to hear.
Stay on one theme. The prompt may be broad; your answer should be narrow and specific.
Ignore the word count on the first draft. Cut later.
Rewrite, then ask one person whose opinion you trust, not six.

reads.title: Six essay topics to avoid, and why
reads.note: Not because they are bad subjects. Thousands of other applicants chose them this year, and it is hard to be specific about a trip to Costa Rica in 650 words.

items.text: Heroism
Death, divorce, depression
The travel itinerary
Religious or political issues
Dating and relationships
Anything you would not want an admissions officer to know

reads.title: The 2026–27 Common App prompts, explained
reads.intro: Seven prompts, 650 words, one essay. The prompts are doors into the same room; pick the one that lets your story walk in naturally.

items.title: Background, identity, interest or talent
items.text: The open door. Works when the thing is specific and you can show it in scenes, not list it.

items.title: A challenge, setback or failure
items.text: The lesson matters more than the failure. Keep the setback to a paragraph and spend the rest on what changed.

items.title: Questioning or challenging a belief
items.text: Not a debate essay. What did you believe, what cracked it, and what do you do differently now?

items.title: Gratitude that surprised you
items.text: Small and specific beats big and vague. One person, one moment.

items.title: An accomplishment or realization that sparked growth
items.text: The realization is the essay. The accomplishment is the setup.

items.title: A topic that makes you lose track of time
items.text: Careful with jargon. The reader should feel the pull, not sit an exam on it.

items.title: Any topic of your choice
items.text: Fine to use, but a great answer to another prompt is usually a great answer here too.

reads.title: Brainstorming questions for the personal statement
reads.intro: Answer these in a page or two, fast and messy. Three or four essay topics usually fall out. Then, for each one, ask: is this mostly about me? Is there a beginning, middle and end? Does it show my best self?

items.text: What is my favorite academic subject, and what memory first sparked it?
What is my greatest success so far? What steps got me there, and how did it feel?
What is my greatest challenge so far? How did I get through it, or how am I getting through it?
What is one talent people would not guess I have? How did I find out?
The activity I pursue with real passion is… and I do it because…
What are my best three character traits, and where do they show up?
How has my family life shaped who I am?
How has my background, culture or country of origin shaped who I am?
The three things (people, places, animals count) that affect me most are… because…
The biggest lesson I have learned so far is… I learned it by… and it made me more…

items.title: Introduction
items.text: A hook, the scene, and a hint of the thesis. Start inside the story, not with a definition of courage.

items.title: Body
items.text: Scenes, not summaries. Show the emotion through action. Skip the bus ride home with a transition and get to the moment that matters.

items.title: Conclusion
items.text: What changed. Or, increasingly, nothing: end the story and let the actions carry the reflection. Most great short stories do.

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: A diary format for a story that spans days. A manifesto. A pivotal essay that opens on the conflict. Structure should fit the story, not the other way round.

items.title: Wordiness
items.text: Most students can cut a quarter of the essay and lose nothing. Try it.

items.title: Vague language
items.text: "Stuff", "things", "this aspect of society". Admissions officers are not mind readers.

items.title: Clichés
items.text: "One in a million." "My global perspective." "My potential as a future leader." If you must use one, put a spin on it.

items.title: Too much "I"
items.text: More than once a sentence is too much. Rearrange the sentence and it usually disappears.

items.title: Adverbs
items.text: "She ran quickly" is "she sprinted". Every adverb is a strong verb waiting to happen.

items.title: Expletive constructions
items.text: "There were two girls who struggled with math" is "two girls struggled with math".

items.title: Flowery language
items.text: Too many adjectives suffocate a paragraph. One precise noun ("a Yorkie") beats three vague ones.
